tagline: From Kīlauea to the sea, on a road lava keeps taking.
intro: The road leaves Crater Rim Drive at Kīlauea in rainforest, at the high end of the east rift zone, and goes down past the string of pit craters it is named for, through Kipuka Nene, where 1,100-year-old trees stand surrounded by fresh lava, and out across pāhoehoe flows toward the coast, 3,700 feet below.

It was dedicated in 1928 on the line of Cockett's Trail and ended then at the rim of Makaopuhi Crater. Lava has been working on it ever since. By 2018 some part of it had been covered in 41 of the previous 53 years, and the Puʻuʻōʻō eruption buried nearly nine miles of road along with the Kamoamoa village site and its black sand beach.

moments.title: Pauahi Crater
moments.text: About three miles down, a pit 300 feet deep where fissures opened across the floor twice in 1973 and once more, for a single day, in 1979.

moments.title: Maunaulu
moments.text: The name means growing mountain, and from 1969 to 1974 it grew, the longest flank eruption Kīlauea had seen in at least 2,200 years, and cut the road.

moments.title: Hōlei Sea Arch
moments.text: Waves cut a 90-foot basalt arch from a lava flow about 550 years old near the end of the road, and it stood until late September 2026, when it fell into the sea.

practical: No food, water or fuel is available along the road; there are vault toilets at the Maunaulu parking area and at the end of the road.

sources.label: National Park Service, Drive Chain of Craters Road
